entities.label: Text
entities.summary:
The Zabur, often referred to as the Book of Psalms in the Judeo-Christian tradition, holds a unique place in Islamic theology as the scripture revealed to Prophet Dawood (David). Although the exact origins of the Zabur are uncertain, it is posited to have emerged around the 10th century BCE in the ancient Near East, specifically within the context of the Israelite kingdom. The significance of the Zabur extends beyond its religious underpinnings; it represents a key intersection of monotheistic traditions, influencing the development of religious texts across cultures and epochs.

The core events surrounding the Zabur center on its revelation to David, who is traditionally considered a pivotal figure in both Jewish and Islamic beliefs. While it is mentioned in the Quran (specifically in Surah Al-Isra, 17:55), the Zabur is acknowledged as a divine book that emphasizes themes of worship, morality, and divine justice. The actual content of the Zabur, preserved mainly in the form of Psalms, consists of poetic hymns and prayers that articulate the human experience in relation to the divine, often addressing themes of lamentation, praise, and supplication, reflecting the spiritual and social issues of its time.

The legacy of the Zabur has profoundly influenced both Islamic and Judeo-Christian traditions, serving as a bridge between these faiths and fostering a shared heritage of sacred music and poetry. As it has been transmitted through generations, the text has inspired countless adaptations, liturgical practices, and artistic expressions, notably its inclusion in Christian worship and its impact on various musical genres. The reverberations of its teachings continue to resonate, as seen in the enduring popularity of the Psalms in contemporary religious life.
